description: How everyday media use builds identity, and the role of fandom and participatory culture in modern media life.
content_html:
Media as Part of Daily Life

Media use is not something that happens in a separate compartment of life — it is woven into everyday routines. People check their phones before getting out of bed, listen to music while commuting, stream video during meals, and scroll social feeds late at night. These media practices are not random: they connect to who people are, who they want to be, and how they relate to others.

Media and Identity: Gauntlett’s Framework

David Gauntlett’s research — most fully developed in Media, Gender and Identity — argues that media use is a key resource through which people actively construct their identity. Rather than simply being told who they are by the media, audiences use media content to explore and develop a sense of self. Gauntlett distinguishes between the actual self and the desired self. Media products can serve both: a viewer might identify with characters who reflect their current identity, or they might be drawn to representations of the person they hope to become.

Gauntlett’s approach contrasts sharply with the passive-audience or hypodermic models. Where earlier effects researchers worried that audiences absorb media values without reflection, Gauntlett argued that the audience is always an active reader, picking and choosing what resonates. Identity construction is ongoing and selective, not a one-time injection.

Key Fact

David Gauntlett argues that audiences use media as a resource for identity construction, drawing on both their actual self (who they currently are) and their desired self (who they want to become). This makes media use an active, ongoing process of self-definition, not passive absorption.

Participatory Culture and Henry Jenkins

Henry Jenkins’ concept of participatory culture describes a media environment in which the boundary between producer and consumer has blurred. In Jenkins’ account, audiences — especially fans — are not content to passively consume media products. They discuss, critique, remix, reimagine and produce their own content in response. This was central to his 1992 book Textual Poachers, where he argued that fans actively “poach” texts, taking elements of existing media products and remaking them according to their own interests and desires.

Jenkins did not frame this as a modern digital phenomenon — fan creativity preceded the internet, through fanzines, fan letters and club meetings. But digital networks have dramatically accelerated the scale and visibility of participatory culture, making fan production (fan fiction, fan videos, commentary channels, cosplay documentation) accessible to millions.

Fandom describes both the state of being a devoted fan and the community that forms around shared devotion to a media product. Fan communities provide a sense of belonging, shared language and social identity. They mobilise around new releases, create rankings, theorise plot developments, and generate enormous amounts of secondary content. In the digital era, fan communities organise rapidly on social platforms, coordinating activities such as streaming events to boost chart positions or directing collective energy towards media organisations.

Contemporary “stan culture” — from the Eminem song “Stan” (2000), now used generically — refers to highly dedicated, sometimes intensely devoted fan behaviour. Stan culture shows both the creative and social power of participatory fandom and some of its less positive dynamics, including harassment of critics, extreme parasocial attachment, and fan communities turning on media creators when their decisions disappoint.

Key Fact

Henry Jenkins’ Textual Poachers (1992) argued that fans are active cultural participants who “poach” texts — taking existing media products and remaking or reimagining them according to their own interests. This is the foundation of participatory culture theory.

Parasocial Relationships and the Watercooler Effect

One of the most striking features of modern media use is the development of parasocial relationships. Audiences develop genuine feelings of familiarity, affection and even grief towards performers, influencers and fictional characters who will never know them. These relationships fulfil real social and psychological needs — particularly the integration and social interaction need identified in Blumler and Katz’s Uses and Gratifications theory.

Media use also generates the watercooler effect: a shared cultural text becomes a topic of conversation, connecting people who otherwise have little in common. A major sporting final, a dramatic episode of a serialised drama, or a divisive viral video all create shared cultural reference points that serve the social function of bringing people into connection with each other.

The Social and Cultural Significance of Media Practices

Media practices have significance beyond entertainment. The media contributes to shared cultural identity by providing common stories, shared news, and collective experiences. It fulfils individual needs for information, companionship and self-expression — particularly important for people who are isolated or who belong to communities not well represented in mainstream media. The ability to access online communities through social platforms and streaming has given niche audiences the opportunity to find each other and build shared culture around media products that mainstream broadcasters would never have commissioned.

Second-screen viewing typifies how media practices have changed in the digital era. Audiences no longer watch in silence: they are simultaneously tweeting reactions, looking up background information, reading other viewers’ responses, and participating in live comment threads. This transforms a traditionally passive act (watching television) into an active social practice. Media producers have responded by designing second-screen tie-ins, companion apps and live social activations around major broadcasts precisely because they know audiences are already doing this.
exam_tip_html: Questions on media practices and identity often reward answers that connect Gauntlett and Jenkins to each other rather than treating them as separate points. Both argue that audiences are active — but Gauntlett focuses on identity construction through selection and identification, while Jenkins focuses on creative production and participatory remaking. If a question uses the command word “discuss,” consider presenting both theorists and then making a judgement about which offers more insight into the specific media form in the question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • David Gauntlett argues that audiences use media as a resource for active identity construction, drawing on their actual self and desired self; this positions audiences as agents in building who they are, not passive recipients of media values.
  • Henry Jenkins’ concept of participatory culture (developed in Textual Poachers, 1992) argues that fans actively “poach” texts, producing fan fiction, videos and commentary — blurring the boundary between audience and producer.
  • Parasocial relationships, the watercooler effect and second-screen viewing all demonstrate the social significance of media practices beyond simple consumption.

practice_questions.text: Which theorist wrote 'Textual Poachers' (1992) and developed the concept of participatory culture?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct answer is A. A) Correct — Henry Jenkins wrote Textual Poachers and developed participatory culture theory. B) Incorrect — David Gauntlett developed identity-construction theory. C) Incorrect — Blumler and Katz developed Uses and Gratifications. D) Incorrect — Gerbner developed cultivation theory.

practice_questions.text: Identify what is meant by the term 'parasocial relationship'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a one-sided relationship in which an audience member feels familiarity or emotional connection with a media personality who does not know they exist.

practice_questions.text: Identify the difference between a person's 'actual self' and 'desired self' in Gauntlett's theory, and explain one way media use can serve each.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: 1 mark for accurately distinguishing actual self (current identity) from desired self (aspirational identity). 1 mark for a developed explanation of how a media product might serve each — for example, a social media user follows accounts that reflect their current interests (actual self) and accounts that represent the lifestyle they aspire to (desired self).

practice_questions.text: Explain what Jenkins means by audiences 'poaching' texts in participatory culture.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Shows awareness that fans create their own content but the connection to Jenkins is vague. Secure: Accurately explains that poaching refers to fans taking elements of existing media products and remaking or reimagining them (fan fiction, fan videos, commentary) according to their own interests, positioning audiences as active cultural participants rather than passive consumers. Mastering: Accurate explanation plus a clear account of why Jenkins saw this as culturally significant — fans are not merely consuming texts but are producing culture themselves, challenging the traditional producer-audience boundary — with a developed example context.

practice_questions.text: Explain how participatory culture and fan practices demonstrate that audiences are active rather than passive.
practice_questions.marks: Developing: Notes that fans do things with media but the explanation of what makes this 'active' is limited. Secure: Explains how fan production (fan fiction, videos, commentary) constitutes active cultural participation; connects to Jenkins' concept of participatory culture and the blurring of producer-audience boundaries. Mastering: Full explanation connecting fan practices to the broader active-audience debate; contrasts with passive-audience models; notes how digital platforms have accelerated the scale of participatory culture without changing its fundamental nature (fan creativity pre-dates the internet per Jenkins).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Gauntlett's theory of identity construction and Jenkins' participatory culture theory together explain the relationship between media use and audience identity in a media form you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names one or both theorists with limited or no connection to a specific media form. Developing: Applies one theory adequately but does not connect the two theories; the link to a specific media form is surface-level. Secure: Applies both theories to a named media form with clear examples; shows how Gauntlett's identity construction and Jenkins' participatory culture are complementary rather than contradictory; uses relevant terminology (actual self, desired self, fan production, parasocial relationship). Mastering: Sustained analytical argument connecting both theories through a specific media form; explicitly links Gauntlett's identity-building function to the motivation for Jenkins' participatory production (fans produce because the text has become part of their identity); considers the social significance of these practices; structured as a coherent argument with a maintained thesis.

knowledge_checks.q: In Gauntlett's theory, which term describes the identity a person aspires to have?
What term describes the social phenomenon where a shared media experience generates conversation among viewers?
Henry Jenkins argued in Textual Poachers (1992) that fans actively _____ texts by taking and remaking elements of existing media products according to their own interests.
A one-sided relationship where an audience member feels familiarity and emotional connection with a media personality who does not know they exist is called a _____ relationship.
Match each theorist to their key concept about audiences.
right: Uses and Gratifications: four audience needs satisfied by media
Participatory culture: audiences as active producers and fans
Identity construction through actual self and desired self

flashcard_questions.q: What is Gauntlett's key argument about media and identity?
flashcard_questions.a: Audiences use media as a resource to actively construct their identity

flashcard_questions.q: In Gauntlett's theory, the 'desired self' is ___.
flashcard_questions.a: The identity a person aspires to have — who they want to become

flashcard_questions.q: Henry Jenkins argued in _____ (1992) that fans actively poach texts.
What does Jenkins mean by fans 'poaching' texts?
flashcard_questions.a: Taking existing media products and remaking them for their own purposes

flashcard_questions.q: What type of relationship forms when an audience member feels familiarity with a media figure who does not know they exist?
The 'watercooler effect' describes how a shared media experience generates _____ among people who watched it.

flashcard_questions.a: Using a second device simultaneously to discuss or look up content while watching television

flashcard_questions.q: Gauntlett's 'actual self' contrasts with the desired self — the actual self is _____.
flashcard_questions.a: The identity a person currently has — who they are now

flashcard_questions.q: In Jenkins' participatory culture, which traditional boundary has been blurred?
flashcard_questions.a: The boundary between producer and audience

flashcard_questions.q: Which of Blumler and Katz's four needs does a parasocial relationship primarily serve?

glossary_terms.definition: The habitual and purposeful ways in which people engage with media products as part of their everyday lives.
The identity a person currently has — who they are as they experience themselves now.
The identity a person aspires to have — who they would like to become.
Henry Jenkins' term for a culture in which audiences are not just consumers but active participants who create, share and contribute to media content.
An organised community of enthusiastic followers of a media product, genre, performer or media figure.
A one-sided relationship in which an audience member feels a sense of intimacy, familiarity and emotional connection with a media personality who does not know they exist.
The social phenomenon where a shared media experience (such as a popular drama episode) generates conversation and debate among people who watched it.
The practice of simultaneously using a second device (typically a smartphone or tablet) to discuss or look up content while watching television.
